extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and developers interested in formalizing mathematics and using Metamath, theorem provers, or proof verifiers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and best practices for installing and using Metamath, integrating (and judging) automated and interactive theorem provers, constructing formal proofs and databases, and choosing axioms/notation when formalizing mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution when trusting computer algebra systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer algebra systems' knowledge databases can be misleading or incomplete (e.g., Mathematica returning discrete n values for Fermat-like queries, Maple missing a non-integer root).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat CAS outputs with caution; they may appear to 'know' deep facts or omit valid solutions. Verify CAS results independently rather than accepting them at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automated theorem provers as search tools, not authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated theorem provers specialize in searching for proofs (often one theorem at a time) and can be excellent tools for those willing to learn how to use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provers to discover candidate proofs, but be prepared to inspect, shorten, or manually rewrite automatically generated proofs before adding them to a database to avoid 'fat and ugly' entries and long verification times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for the learning curve and practicality limits of provers
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated and interactive provers often require experience, skill, patience, and sometimes precise restatement of axioms; many algorithms (e.g., Tarski's) are impractically inefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest time in learning how to use tools like otter/eprover and their methods for obtaining concise proofs; expect that some deep theorems remain difficult for automation and that tools tend to perform well only on relatively easy theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit proof objects when you need verifiable step-by-step proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some interactive theorem provers store 'proofs' as programs or scripts that guide the prover rather than as explicit sequences of proof steps; Metamath stores every step of every proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your objective is archival, independent verification, or human inspection of every inference, choose a system (like Metamath) that records explicit proof steps rather than only tactic scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the distinction: theorem provers vs proof verifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated theorem provers generate proofs; proof verifiers check proofs you provide (often with limited automation). Metamath is primarily a proof verifier and documenter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tools according to whether you need generation (provers) or rigorous verification/archiving (verifiers). Be aware verifiers may include small automation but expect human-guided structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding of mathematical knowledge differs by system
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems embed foundational knowledge in the underlying program (interactive provers), while Metamath places the mathematical knowledge directly in the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the approach that fits your goals: embedded tactics can ease proof construction but reduce portability/explicitness; database-centric systems maximize transparency and portability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect steeper learning curves for high-level proof assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems like HOL Light, Isabelle, hol, and Coq can have a steep learning curve and often require a fair understanding of mathematical logic to follow their proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for several weeks of learning to use such systems effectively; weigh the tradeoff between power of tactics and the cost of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When combining provers with Metamath, prefer concise automated proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Very long, automatically generated proofs can bloat a Metamath database and slow verification; concise outputs are preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using automated provers to produce proofs for Metamath, aim to instruct the prover to find shorter proofs or plan to manually rewrite the output before inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperability and translation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Related proof languages (e.g., Ghilbert) may allow translation of some Metamath materials; community size and tooling differ across systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider available translators and the active community when choosing a system; smaller communities may have less tooling/support but can still interoperate on some artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address obstacles to large-scale formalization projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Large initiatives (e.g., qed) struggled because few people work on formalization, no compelling applications existed, and formalized mathematics did not yet resemble traditional math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To attract contributors and sustain work, seek compelling applications, make formalized mathematics more familiar to mathematicians, and lower barriers to entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic choices should favor simplicity and obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A good axiomatic system states trivial and obvious truths as axioms so that less-obvious results follow unambiguously; the choice of axioms can be partly stylistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select axioms that are simple and minimal; avoid keeping as axioms statements that can be derived, thereby keeping the axiom set small and comprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break axioms into small pieces to avoid metatheorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking standard axioms into smaller pieces can allow derivation of results that would otherwise be metatheorems, making the system more convenient for formal proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design axiom schemes so that commonly needed metatheorems become derivable inside the system; this aids direct formal derivations at the cost of less intuitive-looking axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid primitive notions like free/bound variables where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: By defining concepts like free variable and proper substitution in terms of axioms rather than primitives, one can simplify the underlying formal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If feasible, express these concepts through the axiom system chosen for your Metamath database to reduce primitive machinery; the traditional approach is still possible if preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath's advantages for long-term verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath is not tied to one set of axioms, shows every proof step, has multiple verifier implementations, and uses a very small, fixed language so proofs remain recheckable across versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Metamath when long-term archival, cross-checking by independent implementations, and reproducible verification across versions are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer permissive licensing and open verifiers for trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath's main databases are public domain and the program is open source; multiple verifiers exist in different languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releasing databases and tools under permissive licenses and providing multiple independent verifiers reduces the risk of accepting invalid proofs due to verifier bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep source format simple and portable
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath source files should be plain ASCII text; recommended line length is 79 characters or less; use a monospaced font for editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit with plain text editors, ensure plain-text saving (not rich-text), and adhere to line-length conventions for cross-platform compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide readable presentation outputs via LaTeX or HTML
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset formulas for printing using LaTeX; Metamath can also produce HTML pages via built-in support (help html).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install LaTeX if you need typeset outputs; use the Metamath help html command to produce web pages for browsing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof schemes to represent infinite families of theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving theorem schemes (schemata) allows one proof to represent infinitely many concrete theorems by substituting metavariables with actual terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing, prefer proving schemes where appropriate to compactly represent infinite families; instantiate schemes to get particular theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use condensed detachment and unification concepts appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensed detachment (compact proof notation referencing axioms/rules with implicit substitutions) and unification are central ideas; Metamath uses a simple version of unification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand unification and condensed detachment to work effectively with compact proof notations; consult referenced literature for extensions to first-order logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens as the fundamental inference rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are sequences of theorems where each line is an axiom or derived by modus ponens from earlier lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure formal proofs so each step is either an axiom instance or obtained by MP; this makes mechanical verification straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restate axioms for compatibility with certain provers
rubrics_metrics.description: To use systems like otter, axioms may need restatement (e.g., eliminating dummy variables) to be compatible and amenable to automated search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow recommended transformations (see comments/references) when exporting or translating axioms for use with particular automated provers to improve effectiveness.
